The energy transition is about acceleration, how quickly we can scale renewable integration. Digital, #data, and AI enable that speed — but we must not trade quickness for justice.

In Skopje this week during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, I questioned, how can we shift the conversation from digital optimization to digital integrity?

#AI can now forecast grid conditions in near real time, anticipate renewable variability, and optimize power flows across billions of data points. Predictive analytics alone could unlock 175 GW of transmission capacity and cut peak loads by 12% — proof that digital systems can make grids both efficient and smarter.

But the faster we move, the less time we leave to verify the quality, origin, and bias of the data itself. In 2024, 4,875 cyber incidents were recorded across the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors — a sharp reminder that every new sensor and data link can also be an entry point for risk. And as 83 percent of urban residents are online compared with just 48 percent of rural populations, the same connectivity gaps that divide access also shape the data that train AI models.

Without open, interoperable, and verifiable systems, we risk building a transition that is more efficient — but not more equitable.

The technologies exist. What’s missing is sustained political will and coordination to ensure that data, AI, and markets work for people, not just performance. The #energy transition will not be powered by technology alone — but by the integrity of the systems and data it rests on.
